title: STABLE: Shift-Tolerant Portfolio via Diffusion and Black-Litterman
one_liner: When market regimes shift, use a generative model to imagine stock returns under the current regime, then let portfolio theory pick the safest mix.
lead: Stock markets change personality: in good times, all boats rise together; in recessions, correlations flip and safe stocks become risky. Picking a portfolio that works in any regime is hard. STABLE does it by first using a generative model (diffusion) to imagine what each stock will return given the macroeconomic conditions right now, then feeds those imagined returns into Black-Litterman portfolio theory, which spreads your money across stocks to balance return and risk.

problem.h2: Why old portfolio theory breaks in a changing market
paras: Pick a portfolio in January using the patterns from the past 10 years. Then a pandemic hits in March and everything changes: oil tanks, some stocks stay safe, others crumble. Your portfolio gets wiped out.

This happens because old portfolio theory (the standard way to pick stock mixes) assumes the world stays the same. It looks back at 10 years of returns and says, 'Here is how risky each stock is; here is how they move together.' Then it spreads your money to balance return and risk. But if market conditions flip, those old patterns are useless.
A beginner might try: just pick the stocks that have been safest for the longest. But that does not work—the safest past stocks are often the riskiest in the next regime, because correlations flip.

callout.html: Picking a safe portfolio is impossible if you do not know what regime the market is in right now.

steps.text: Feed macroeconomic data (unemployment, interest rates, oil prices) into the model.
Generative model imagines what each stock's returns could be given that regime.
Extract the mean return and covariance (how returns move together) from the imagined futures.
Black-Litterman module weights stocks to maximize risk-adjusted return.
Allocate money according to the weights; recompute daily as regime signals change.

paras: The paper changes the input estimates fed to portfolio theory: instead of using fixed historical statistics, it uses regime-aware return predictions from a generative model.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: the market regime
hidden.name: Market regime (macro conditions)
paras: A market regime is the personality of markets right now: booming and stable, or in recession and volatile, or stagflation-plagued. It is invisible—you cannot point to it like a stock price. But macroeconomic data (unemployment, interest rates, sentiment surveys) hint at which regime you are in.

STABLE uses the macroeconomic context as input and tunes the generative model to produce imagined stock returns that are consistent with that regime. The model learns to say: 'If unemployment is rising and the Fed is hiking, growth stocks will tank and bonds will shine.' The regime signal is embedded in the model's choices of what returns to imagine.

heat.caption: Darker cells show which asset types thrive in each regime. The heat map shifts as macro conditions change.

reads.html: The regime is 'the mode the market is in right now.' When unemployment is high and interest rates are falling, we are in a different regime than when unemployment is low and rates are rising. Different regimes favor different stock types.

STABLE learns a conditional generative model that produces per-stock return trajectories reflecting the macroeconomic context. The model conditions on the regime signal embedded in the macro inputs and produces regime-coherent forecasts.

mechanism.h2: Why regime-aware estimates fix the problem
paras: Old portfolio theory uses one set of statistics (average return, volatility, correlations) computed from 10 years of history. It does not know that correlations are different in booms and busts. So it makes mistakes: it recommends stocks that were safe in the last regime but will blow up in the next.

STABLE's generative model learns to imagine stock returns as a function of the macro regime. When the model sees 'recession signals' in the input, it generates imagined futures where bond-like stocks do well and cyclical stocks tank. Those regime-specific imagined futures become the inputs to Black-Litterman portfolio theory.

Black-Litterman then spreads your money to maximize risk-adjusted return using the correct regime-specific estimates. Because the estimates now match reality (the regime the market is actually in), the portfolio adapts—it survives regime shifts instead of being blindsided.

stages.s: Generative model imagines regime-specific return futures
Extract mean return and covariance from imagined data
Black-Litterman balances stocks by risk and return
Portfolio weights that fit the regime

math.words: Weight for stock i equals a base weight, adjusted up by a confidence-weighted view of that stock's return relative to the market average.
math.equation: w_i = w_market_i + (1 / lambda) * Sigma^{-1} * (mu_view_i - mu_market_i) / sigma_view_i^2
symbols: final weight (fraction of portfolio) for stock i
baseline weight for stock i (e.g., equal-weighted)
predicted return for stock i from generative model
uncertainty in that prediction (lower is more confident)
a table showing how each pair of stocks moves together

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose the market average return is 8%. Generative model predicts Stock A returns 12% (confident) and Stock B returns 9% (uncertain).
Black-Litterman sees Stock A's edge (12% vs 8%) is real and weights it higher.
Stock B's tiny edge (9% vs 8%) is uncertain, so it barely budges from the baseline.
If macro regime shifts and predictions change, the weights recompute daily: no portfolio is fixed for 10 years.

math.note: The formula says: start with a baseline portfolio, then tilt toward stocks the regime-aware model predicts will do well, adjusting confidence based on how certain that prediction is.

charts.title: Old method (fixed history)
charts.note: Uses 10 years of static history; broken in regime shifts.

charts.title: STABLE (regime-aware)
charts.note: Regime-aware estimates protect in busts and still capture upside in booms.

items.b: Macro data is lagged or wrong.
items.html: If unemployment data comes out two weeks late or Fed signals are misread, the regime signal is stale. The model imagines returns for the wrong regime, and the portfolio is misaligned. Fix: use higher-frequency sentiment data or explicit regime-switching models.

items.b: Generative model has not seen that regime before.
items.html: If a financial crisis is brand new (e.g., pandemic), the model was trained on historical data it never saw. Its imagined returns are plausible but not accurate. Fix: calibrate confidence; do not trust predictions in regimes outside training data.

In panic crashes, correlations all converge to 1 (everything falls together). The Black-Litterman module assumes covariances are stable, so diversification fails when needed most. Fix: use dynamic covariance models or limit the fraction of money put into any one position.

Regime signals are updated daily from real-time macro data, confidence intervals are wide for regimes outside training, and the portfolio is stress-tested on historical crises. Rebalancing is gradual to avoid whipsaw.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Take three years of daily market data from 2020 through 2023, covering boom, COVID crash, and recovery. Split into train and test. Train the generative model on year 1 and 2. On year 3, compare: (1) a naive portfolio built on year 1 data only, (2) STABLE re-estimating regime and re-weighting daily. Measure which one has higher Sharpe ratio and lower max drawdown over year 3.
demo.metric_eq: Sharpe ratio = (mean daily return - risk-free rate) / daily volatility; max drawdown = (peak value - trough value) / peak value.
demo.closing: STABLE's portfolio should have lower drawdown in the COVID crash (because the regime signal switched) and similar or better Sharpe ratio overall.
